title: The Interrogation Rooms
question: Two suspects, no communication: both silent gives 1 year each; both betray gives 3 each; lone betrayer walks while the loyal gets 5. If both reason selfishly and rationally, what happens?
choices: One betrays while the other stays silent
correctExplanation: Both betray — defecting dominates: whatever the other does, betraying pays better individually. Mutual betrayal is the Nash equilibrium both regret.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is both betray, serving 3 years each. Check each cell: if your partner stays silent, betraying walks you (0 beats 1); if they betray, betraying cuts 5 to 3. Dominance decides regardless of sympathy.
lessonContent:
Dominant strategies decide regardless of sympathy.
Equilibria can be regretted by everyone inside them.
Individual rationality aggregates into collective folly.
Map every cell before trusting solidarity.

title: The Copycat Champion
question: Axelrod's computer tournaments pitted dozens of strategies in repeated dilemmas. Which disarmingly simple rule won twice?
choices: Tit-for-tat: cooperate first, then copy the opponent
correctAnswer: Tit-for-tat: cooperate first, then copy the opponent
correctExplanation: Tit-for-tat — nice, retaliatory, forgiving, clear. It never beats opponents head-to-head yet outscores them across tournaments by eliciting cooperation.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is tit-for-tat: cooperate first, then copy the opponent. Defection wins battles; reciprocity wins tournaments. Clarity plus forgiveness outscored every clever exploitation scheme entered.
lessonContent:
Nice, clear, retaliatory, forgiving: the winning quartet.
Tournaments reward eliciting, not extracting.
Simplicity beats cleverness across populations.
Copycats inherit cooperative worlds.

title: The Long Shadow
question: One-shot dilemmas end in betrayal, but repeated ones sustain cooperation. What does repetition add that changes everything?
choices: The rules rewrite themselves over time
correctExplanation: Future retaliation — the shadow of coming rounds prices today's betrayal. Cooperation becomes self-interest once tomorrows matter.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is future retaliation disciplines present defection. Friendship, rule changes, and growing stakes are optional; consequences are structural. Lengthen shadows and cooperation follows.
lessonContent:
Shadows of future rounds price present moves.
Consequences, not character, sustain cooperation.
Lengthen interactions to lengthen honesty.
Tomorrows mattering changes todays completely.

title: The Shared Pasture
question: Herder logic: adding one more cow gains its owner the full animal while the overgrazing cost spreads across all herders. What makes this rational individually and ruinous collectively?
choices: Each herder gains fully while sharing the damage
correctAnswer: Each herder gains fully while sharing the damage
correctExplanation: Full gains, shared damage — privatized benefits with socialized costs drive every herder to overstock. The pasture dies of individually sensible decisions.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is each herder gains fully while sharing the damage. Bans, fights, and weather miss the mechanism: asymmetric accounting. When I keep the cow and we share the bald field, baldness is arithmetic.
lessonContent:
Privatized gains plus socialized costs ruin commons.
Asymmetric accounting drives overuse everywhere.
Sensible individuals compose ruined collectives.
Fix accounting before blaming herders.

title: The Lobster Norms
question: Maine lobstermen sustain catches for generations while open-access fisheries collapse. Researchers credit community enforcement, not just biology. What sustains the Maine catch?
correctExplanation: Local monitoring plus graduated sanctions — Ostrom's design: watched waters plus penalties that escalate. Norms with teeth outlast fences without watchers.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is local monitoring plus graduated sanctions. Biology, feds, and temperature miss it: communities that watch and punish proportionally sustain what open access liquidates. Institutions, not oceans, decide.
lessonContent:
Watched waters sustain what open access liquidates.
Penalties escalating beat punishments binary.
Institutions decide where biology merely enables.
Norms need teeth to hold teeth (lobster).

title: The Free Listener
question: Public radio is funded by voluntary pledges, yet non-payers hear every broadcast. What economic problem does the station face?
correctExplanation: Free-riding — broadcasts can't exclude non-payers, so self-interest says listen free. Voluntary funding fights equilibrium constantly.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is free-riding on non-excludable goods. Storms, regulators, and podcasts orbit the core: excludability missing means payment optional means underfunding chronic. Pledge drives beg against equilibria.
lessonContent:
Non-excludable goods invite unpaid use.
Optional payment means chronic underfunding.
Pledge drives beg against equilibria.
Design funding that doesn't need angels.

title: The Rejected Dollar
question: A proposer splits $10; the responder can veto, leaving both with nothing. Pure rationality accepts even $1 — yet most humans reject low offers. What does rejection reveal?
choices: Fairness preferences overruling pure payoff maximization
correctAnswer: Fairness preferences overruling pure payoff maximization
correctExplanation: Fairness overrules maximization — responders pay to punish insulting splits. Utility includes dignity, not just dollars.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is fairness preferences overruling pure payoff maximization. Innumeracy, confusion, and spite miss it: costly punishment of unfairness is principled, predictable, and cross-cultural. Dollars aren't the only currency.
lessonContent:
Dignity prices into every split offered.
Costly punishment polices fairness norms.
Utility includes insult, not just income.
Vetoes speak where acceptance would profit.

title: The Quiet Gift
question: A dictator splits $10 with a passive recipient who must accept anything. Pure rationality gives $0 — yet average gifts hover near $3. What does giving show?
correctExplanation: Prosocial preferences without enforcement — dictators share with ghosts who cannot retaliate. Generosity precedes incentives.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is prosocial preferences operating without enforcement. No retaliation threatens, no error explains, no staff pays: giving flows from internalized norms. Humans arrive pre-loaded with fairness.
lessonContent:
Generosity precedes incentives developmentally.
Ghosts receive real money from real dictators.
Internalized norms pay without police.
Pre-loaded fairness beats pure selfishness.

title: The Tripled Trust
question: An investor sends money that triples en route; the trustee may return any share. Strangers routinely send generously and receive fairly back. What sustains this?
correctExplanation: Reciprocity plus reputational shadow — trust extended expects return, and social worlds punish betrayal. Tripling tempts; norms restrain.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is reciprocity norms plus reputational shadow. No contracts bind, no twins play, no fakes circulate: strangers trust because social species keep ledgers. Returns reward the brave senders.
lessonContent:
Social species keep invisible ledgers always.
Tripling tempts; norms restrain reliably.
Trust extended expects return by default.
Shadows of reputation discipline strangers.

title: The Shaky Partner
question: Two hunters can jointly take a stag (feast) or solo a hare (snack). If your partner might wander, what tempts you toward the smaller prize?
choices: The safe hare when the partner seems shaky
correctAnswer: The safe hare when the partner seems shaky
correctExplanation: The safe hare — stag pays best only with trusted coordination; doubt discounts it. Risk-dominant safety beats payoff-dominant glory under uncertainty.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the safe hare when the partner seems shaky. Laziness, taste, and superstition miss it: trust levels select equilibria. Rousseau's hunters teach that confidence coordinates, doubt defects.
lessonContent:
Trust levels select equilibria directly.
Confidence coordinates; doubt defects.
Safety tempts exactly when partners wobble.
Payoff-dominance needs trust to activate.

title: The Headlight Game
question: Two drivers race straight at each other; first to swerve loses face, neither swerving wrecks both. Nuclear crises ran this exact script. What game is this?
correctExplanation: Chicken — winning means convincing the other you'll never swerve. Brinkmanship weaponizes apparent irrationality: the stronger the commitment, the stronger the leverage.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is chicken: brinkmanship with catastrophic ties. Cooperation, dances, and grids mislabel it: losers swerve, winners risk everything, ties kill. Credible craziness is the equilibrium strategy.
lessonContent:
Credible craziness leverages rational opponents.
Swerve-losses price against crash-losses.
Commitment devices win staring contests.
Apparent irrationality can be strategy.

title: The Station Meeting
question: Separated partners must reunite somewhere in New York with zero communication. Most pairs independently choose the same famous spot at noon. What coordinated them?
choices: A focal point salient to both minds
correctAnswer: A focal point salient to both minds
correctExplanation: A focal point — Grand Central at noon stands out symmetrically: each expects the other to expect it. Salience substitutes for communication.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is a focal point salient to both minds. No telepathy, agreements, or trackers: shared culture makes one option conspicuous to both. Schelling points coordinate the incommunicado.
lessonContent:
Salience substitutes for communication elegantly.
Shared culture spotlights meeting places.
Expectations of expectations converge fast.
Conspicuous options coordinate strangers.

title: The Side Choice
question: A country must standardize driving on the left or the right; either works if everyone complies. What kind of solution does this need?
choices: Scientific proof of the better side
correctExplanation: A shared convention — coordination needs agreement, not optimality. Left and right tie on merits; unanimity breaks all ties.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a shared convention, either side. Science, history, and instinct miss it: content is arbitrary, commonality essential. Conventions solve by synchronizing, never by optimizing.
lessonContent:
Agreement beats optimality in coordination.
Arbitrary content, essential commonality.
Conventions synchronize; they never optimize.
Unanimity breaks all substantive ties.

title: The Pump War
question: Two gas stations undercut each other until margins hit zero, though both earned more at high prices. What trapped these competitors?
choices: Mutual defection as the only equilibrium
correctAnswer: Mutual defection as the only equilibrium
correctExplanation: Mutual defection — each station must undercut whatever the rival charges, so prices ratchet to cost. Preferred outcomes aren't equilibria.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is mutual defection as the only equilibrium. Oil, loyalty, and regulators orbit the core: unilateral high prices get undercut instantly. Preferred matrices collapse without enforcement.
lessonContent:
Preferred outcomes collapse without enforcement.
Undercutting ratchets prices to cost.
Unilateral virtue gets punished promptly.
Equilibria ignore everyone's preferences.

title: The Secret Barrel
question: Cartel members pledge output quotas to hold prices high, yet each can profit by secretly pumping extra at the cartel price. What tempts every member?
choices: Full price for one's own extra barrels
correctAnswer: Full price for one's own extra barrels
correctExplanation: Full price for secret extras — the cheater sells cartel-priced oil in cartel-breaking volume. Quotas bind everyone except, marginally, you.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is full price for one's own extra barrels. Loyalty, boycotts, and meetings miss the math: extra volume at held-high prices is irresistible individually, fatal collectively. Cartels die of private arithmetic.
lessonContent:
Private arithmetic kills public agreements.
Held prices plus secret volume tempts all.
Quotas bind everyone except marginally you.
Cartels need monitors, not just handshakes.

title: The Smokestack Pact
question: Two hundred nations all gain if all cut emissions, while each gains most by polluting as others cut. Climate talks stall in exactly this structure. What is it?
choices: A coordination game with easy fixes
correctExplanation: An N-player prisoner's dilemma — universal cutting beats universal polluting, but defecting dominates each seat. Scale multiplies the original two-person trap.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is an N-player prisoner's dilemma. Misunderstandings and easy fixes deny the structure: every nation faces the interrogation room with 199 partners. Treaties must rewrite payoffs, not just plead.
lessonContent:
Scale multiplies classic traps undiminished.
Two-person logic governs 200-seat rooms.
Pleadings fail where payoffs rule.
Treaties must rewrite, never merely request.

title: The Miracle Jar
question: Each antibiotic course cures its patient while slightly eroding drug effectiveness for everyone future. What kind of good is antibiotic effectiveness?
choices: A commons depleted by individually rational use
A private good owned by pharmacists
correctAnswer: A commons depleted by individually rational use
correctExplanation: A depleting commons — each prescription is correct for its patient and corrosive for the future. Effectiveness is shared pasture grazed by prescriptions.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a commons depleted by individually rational use. Ownership, infinity, and luxury misclassify: cures consume future cures. Stewardship means sometimes withholding working drugs.
lessonContent:
Cures consume future cures measurably.
Correct-for-patient can corrode-for-all.
Shared pastures include invisible medicines.
Stewardship sometimes withholds working drugs.

title: The Pledge Threshold
question: A fundraiser charges cards only if 500 donors join — nobody risks paying alone for a failed project. What mechanism removes the sucker's risk?
correctExplanation: A dominant assurance contract — pledging is safe (no charge if short) and decisive (your pledge may complete the threshold). Tabarrok's fix makes cooperation the easy choice.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is a dominant assurance contract. Guilt, fame, and prizes orbit the core mechanism: conditional charging deletes downside while preserving upside. Assure first, collect after.
lessonContent:
Conditional charging deletes downside risk.
Thresholds convert pledges into pivotal acts.
Assure first; collect only on success.
Mechanisms beat moralizing for funding.

title: The Eternal Grudge
question: One strategy cooperates until any defection, then defects forever after. In repeated games, what does this grim posture threaten?
correctExplanation: Permanent retaliation — one strike ends cooperation eternally. Grim threats sustain peace precisely by being unthinkable to trigger.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is permanent retaliation for any deviation. Forgiveness variants soften other strategies; grim's whole power is irreversibility. Eternity deters what proportion forgets.
lessonContent:
Irreversibility deters what proportion forgets.
Eternal threats sustain fragile peaces.
One strike ends worlds under grim rules.
Unthinkable consequences govern thinkable acts.

title: The Forgiving Copy
question: In noisy tournaments where moves get misread, plain copycatting spirals into endless feuds from single errors. What modification wins instead?
correctExplanation: Occasional forgiveness — generous tit-for-tat absorbs errors instead of echoing them. Noise demands shock absorbers, not louder echoes.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is occasional forgiveness breaking retaliation spirals. Never-retaliate gets exploited, harsher echoes amplify static, quitting forfeits everything. Generosity is error-correction for strategies.
lessonContent:
Noise demands shock absorbers in strategies.
Echoes amplify static; forgiveness filters it.
Errors need absorption, never mirroring.
Generosity error-corrects retaliation.

title: The Staying Rule
question: Win-stay-lose-shift repeats whatever just paid and abandons whatever just failed — no memory beyond last round. Under noisy conditions this outperforms copycatting. What is the rule?
choices: Stay on wins, shift on losses
correctAnswer: Stay on wins, shift on losses
correctExplanation: Stay on wins, shift on losses — Pavlov corrects its own mistakes where tit-for-tat echoes noise. One-round memory beats grudges in static.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is stay on wins, shift on losses. Initial cooperation, rigidity, and double-copying miss it: outcome-contingent switching self-repairs. Pavlov salivates at rewards and abandons punishments.
lessonContent:
Outcome-contingent switching self-repairs fast.
One-round memory beats eternal grudges.
Rewards repeated; punishments abandoned.
Simplicity with feedback beats memory with spite.

title: The Good Name
question: Donors give generously to strangers known to have given to others — cooperation sustained without any repeated meetings. What mechanism carries it?
correctExplanation: Indirect reciprocity — image scores circulate: help the helpful, and helpers help you. Reputation extends reciprocity beyond pairs.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is indirect reciprocity through reputations. Kinship, welfare, and force miss it: strangers cooperate via gossip ledgers. 'I help you because you helped them' scales kindness to societies.
lessonContent:
Gossip ledgers scale kindness to societies.
Image scores circulate like currency.
Help-the-helpful rules need no repeats.
Reputation extends reciprocity past pairs.

title: The Fixed Split
question: Press and Dyson discovered strategies letting one player unilaterally enforce a fixed, unfair payoff ratio against any adapting opponent. What do these extortionate strategies enforce?
correctExplanation: A lopsided ratio, unilaterally — zero-determinant strategies pin the opponent's payoff to your own terms. Mathematics permits what morals condemn.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a lopsided payoff ratio unilaterally. Equality, welfare, and fairness miss it: extortionate ZD play sets the exchange rate by fiat. Opponents adapt; the ratio stands.
lessonContent:
Mathematics permits what morals condemn.
Ratios set by fiat survive adaptation.
Unilateral pinning beats mutual bargaining.
Exchange rates can be dictated, not just dealt.

title: The Tipping Pool
question: In collective-risk experiments, groups facing a catastrophic tipping point contribute far more when the danger is high, clear, and shared. What drives the contributions?
choices: Perceived catastrophic risk with clear thresholds
correctAnswer: Perceived catastrophic risk with clear thresholds
correctExplanation: Perceived catastrophic risk with clear thresholds — Milinski's pools fill when doom is vivid and the line visible. Clarity plus stakes manufacture cooperation.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is perceived catastrophic risk with clear thresholds. Selflessness, mandates, and ignorance miss it: transparent danger focuses minds that foggy danger frees. Draw bright lines around cliffs.
lessonContent:
Bright lines around cliffs focus minds.
Vivid doom funds prevention generously.
Foggy dangers free-ride; clear ones compel.
Thresholds convert crowds into crews.

title: The Costly Ballot
question: A single vote essentially never decides large elections, yet millions pay real costs to cast one. What best explains mass turnout?
choices: Expressive and norm-driven motives beyond pivotality
correctAnswer: Expressive and norm-driven motives beyond pivotality
correctExplanation: Expressive and norm-driven motives — voters speak values and honor duty; pivotality never enters it. Ballots are voices, not levers.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is expressive and norm-driven motives beyond pivotality. Innumeracy, bribery, and coercion miss most turnout: citizens vote to be the kind of people who vote. Identity outbids instrumentality at the polls.
lessonContent:
Identity outbids instrumentality at polls.
Ballots voice values; they rarely lever outcomes.
Duty speaks where pivotality stays silent.
Vote to be voters, not to decide.
